Net worth by age: read Canadian medians without turning them into targets

Four charts connect dated Canadian wealth statistics with a separate household balance sheet, showing why a large net worth can still leave a short cash runway.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate survey benchmarks from your own cash position

Interactive planning lab

Illustrative net worth, before realization costs$627,000
Accessible cash after the entered bills$7,000
Bills without accessible cash funding$0

The first two charts are fixed public survey observations, not a current wealth ranking or a savings target. Age follows the major income recipient. The survey includes economic families and persons outside economic families in the ten provinces; it excludes Indigenous communities and collective dwellings and underrepresents very high wealth. All survey amounts, including 2019, are expressed in constant 2023 dollars. Sampling variability applies; this release table supplies no confidence intervals. The separate household example uses nominal CAD today, not inflation-adjusted survey dollars. Home equity is already net of its mortgage; exclude that mortgage from other debt. The separately estimated pension value is an asset amount, not annual income or an accessible account. Existing due bills must not also appear in other debt. Investments, property and pension assets are not automatically converted to cash. No tax, sale cost or benefit eligibility is calculated.

The central idea

A wealth median describes a group. A workable financial plan also needs your bill dates, accessible cash, future income and goals.

01

Read the age groups as snapshots, not a personal finish line

The first chart compares median net worth in five age groups from Statistics Canada’s 2023 Survey of Financial Security. The age belongs to the family’s major income recipient. Each observation covers economic families and people outside an economic family; it is not a per-adult account balance.

The source expresses both survey years in constant 2023 dollars. This matters: the 2019 bars have already been adjusted for the price level. Treating their difference from 2023 as a nominal investment return would mix unlike concepts. The first chart deliberately retains that same dollar basis.

People in the 35-to-44 group in one survey do not form the identical group four years later. Some have moved into another age category; household composition has changed; some assets have changed in value. The comparison is therefore a description of groups at two dates, rather than evidence that an individual saver should have experienced the same increase.

02

A median is a location in a distribution, not an amount everyone needs

The median sits at the middle of an ordered distribution. It does not describe the range around that middle, show how far apart two neighbouring families are, or tell you the percentile of an arbitrary amount you enter. These charts do not invent a percentile calculator from a handful of medians.

The second chart changes the comparison unit. A two-person family and a person living outside an economic family can have different expenses, years of earning, asset ownership and pension arrangements. Comparing their medians does not isolate a causal effect of household size.

The survey covers the ten provinces with the exclusions described in the source notes. It is a sample, with sampling variability, and it does not represent the very highest wealth adequately. The cited release table supplies no confidence intervals for these displayed medians. Keep those coverage limits alongside the graphic rather than treating the bars as a complete census.

03

Put your own assets and debts on a different page of the plan

The third chart is an editable household example, expressed in dollars today. It is separate from the official statistics. It adds cash, other investments, home equity and an independently estimated workplace pension asset, then deducts other debt and existing bills due before the next income receipt.

Home equity already means home value less its mortgage. Entering the mortgage again under other debt would count the liability twice. Similarly, an annual pension benefit is an income amount, not a pension asset valuation. A plan statement or a qualified valuation may be needed before using an asset figure. Do not count the same entitlement through two different fields.

The original example gives an illustrative net worth of CAD 627,000. That total excludes realization costs and taxes. It is not a prediction of what a sale would produce, an assessment of retirement adequacy, or a direct comparison with constant-2023-dollar survey observations. A pension valuation, a property interest and a bank balance also have different access conditions.

04

Ask which assets can actually fund the next bill

In the original example, CAD 15,000 of accessible cash faces CAD 8,000 of existing bills before the next income. That leaves CAD 7,000. At CAD 3,500 of subsequent monthly essentials, the cash-only runway is two months. The much larger net-worth total cannot pay a bill by itself.

The fourth chart varies the near-term bills and monthly essentials while holding accessible cash fixed. It does not liquidate investments, borrow against the home or convert the pension into a lump sum. A zero cell can mean the cash has simply been used up; when bills exceed cash, the separate unfunded-bills metric shows the immediate problem.

The entered bills are existing liabilities. The monthly essentials describe spending after those bills, so avoid entering the same expense in both places. This is a static coverage measure, with no new income, sale proceeds, investment return or tax calculation. Adding an actual income calendar is the next step before choosing a reserve target.

05

Use benchmarks to improve the questions in your review

Begin with what the money must accomplish. A household expecting pension income, a renter funding every housing payment from investments, and an owner planning to move can need different portfolios even at the same age and net worth. A survey median cannot settle any of those cash-flow questions.

  1. Record assets, liabilities and the date of each valuation.
  2. Separate accessible cash from assets needing a sale, withdrawal or formal approval.
  3. List bills due before the next income and identify any funding gap.
  4. Map recurring spending against reliable future income.
  5. Review tax, ownership and access before counting an asset toward a dated goal.

Update the household figures as circumstances change while keeping the official charts attached to their original survey years. A newer retrieval date does not turn a 2023 observation into a current estimate. The most useful benchmark is one that helps you ask a better planning question and then answer it with your own dated evidence.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. The worked examples, scenario assumptions, and research checklists are TickerLantern’s own educational analysis; they are not source-reported investment results. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Survey of Financial Security, 2023, Table 1 ↗

    Released 29 October 2024; retrieved 25 October 2026. Fourteen retained median observations: five age groups and two family-unit groups, for 2019 and 2023. The charts use twelve of those observations. All amounts are constant 2023 Canadian dollars. Extraction checks the original column headers, units, row uniqueness and HTML SHA-256.

  2. Statistics Canada · Survey of Financial Security, 2023: release and notes ↗

    Defines the survey unit, net worth, population coverage, sampling variability and the limits of representing very high wealth. These are dated survey observations, not 2026 estimates or targets.
